title: The five rulings

cards: A small stick of wood, frayed at one end, used to clean the teeth: the siwak.

In Sahih al-Bukhari, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, says that if it would not be too hard on his community, he would have ordered them to use it at every prayer. And he held back from making it a command.
Between a command and nothing at all, there's a whole range, and that one sentence sits right in the middle of it. Today: what all the sources produce.

teach.b: The word is ahkam, rulings, the plural of hukm.

teach.h: FIVE KINDS OF ACTS, FROM DUTY TO BAN.
teach.b: Jurists sort every human act into five kinds. First, obligatory: the prescribed prayers, the fast of Ramadan. Doing it brings reward; leaving it brings blame.
Second, recommended: the siwak, extra prayers, smiling at someone. Doing it brings reward, but leaving it brings no blame. That's where the Prophet placed the siwak, out of mercy.
Third, permitted: eating an apple, taking a walk, choosing blue over green. No reward, no blame, just life. Fourth, disliked: wasting water while washing for prayer is an example jurists give.
Leaving it brings reward, but doing it brings no sin. Fifth, forbidden: theft, lying to cheat someone. Doing it brings blame.
The scale turns religion from a switch, allowed or not, into a dial. A person who keeps the obligatory and avoids the forbidden is inside the law.
The recommended is an invitation to go further, and the disliked a gentle warning, not a wall.

Sunni and Shia jurists both use these five. In Ja'fari books the names are wajib, mustahabb, mubah, makruh, haram. Sunni books use the same, with some synonyms, like fard for obligatory and mandub for recommended.
The Hanafi school draws finer lines: it separates fard from wajib by how certain the evidence is, and splits the disliked into a lighter kind and a heavier one.
This week traced where rulings come from: the sunnah, agreement, likeness, reason, the common good, custom.
The five are what they produce, and the siwak shows the spirit: the one who brought the law held back from a duty, because a duty is heavy.

how: Muslim jurists, Sunni and Shia, sort acts into obligatory, recommended, permitted, disliked and forbidden, and books of practical rulings label each act with one of these.

games.q: the Prophet could make the siwak a command at every prayer. what does he do?
o: he commands it at every prayer.

games.why: he said he would have ordered it, if it weren't too hard on his community. so it stays recommended, out of mercy.

practice: Pick three things you did yesterday, something you ate, something you said, something you did with your hands, and without judging yourself, place each one on the dial. Notice how many land in the wide middle, the simply permitted.
